# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–26 (Complete – Updated 186)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Summer of seventh year** (Chapter 26). John Sedley dying. Major Dobbin returned to England, reunited with Amelia. Rawdon governs Coventry Island. Georgy established at Russell Square with grandfather.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 24 opened "winter of sixth year"; Chapter 25 opened "spring of seventh year"; Chapter 26 opens "summer of seventh year."
- **Major locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Conduit Street, Hart Street Bloomsbury, Southampton Row, Kensington Gardens, Camberwell, Slaughters' Inn, Haymarket Theatre, Gillespie Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Piccadilly; Madras; St. Helena; Cape; Southampton; Belgium (Brussels, Mount St. John); Bengal; Salford; Regent's Park.

## The Duel and Its Resolution (Chapter 23–24)
**Duel Outcome**: Secret rencontre between Rawdon and Steyne; outcome buried "in profoundest oblivion" by agreement but story spread rapidly. Scandal suppressed from newspapers by Wagg acting on Wenham's hint.

**Rawdon's Refusal of Reconciliation**: Refused Pitt's reconciliation message. Rebecca concealed money ten years; Rawdon declared he would never see her again, "If she's not guilty, Pitt, she's as bad as guilty."

**Rawdon's Acceptance of Governorship**: Initially resisted Steyne's gift. Persuaded by Pitt and especially Macmurdo's argument that accepting position would spite Steyne by making him instrument of Rawdon's prosperity.

## Rebecca's Fate (Chapter 24)
Bailiffs seized Curzon Street property. Rawdon made Rebecca "tolerable annuity." Her whereabouts unknown; "Who cared!"

## Rawdon's Transformation (Chapter 24)
Governor of Coventry Island, three thousand per year. Complete moral transformation: maintains honor, fulfills obligations, provides for son's education, compensates those wronged.

## Georgy Osborne (Chapter 24–25)
**Establishment**: "Fairly established in his grandfather's mansion in Russell Square," heir apparent to splendours. Mr. Osborne "as proud of him as ever" of elder George.

**Character and Dominance**: Scarcely eleven years old. Superior education made him "much better gentleman" than grandfather; boy's "quick brain" revealed grandfather "a dullard." Boy began commanding grandfather, who "was afraid of Georgy." Dressed daily for dinner as "West End swell" with straps, boots, gilt spurs, gold-headed whip. One domestic attended him. After breakfast, read Morning Post "like a grown-up man." Made house lively by activity, imperiousness, scolding, good-nature.

**School and Academics**: Day boy at Reverend Lawrence Veal's School (Hart Street, Bloomsbury). Veal is domestic Chaplain to Earl of Bareacres. Marked aristos in Greek, optimus in Latin, très bien in French. Schoolboys call Veal "Longtail"—name Georgy gave him.

**Friendships**: Young Todd of Coram Street was Georgy's great friend. Both attended principal theatres, knew actors' names. **Mrs. Todd's plan (rumor)**: Privately wondered if Georgy and her daughter Rosa Jemima "might happen."

**Admiration for Dobbin (Chapter 25)**: "Georgy never tired of his praises" to mother. Told Amelia Dobbin "knows such lots of things" and "reads Latin like English." Heard Colonel Buckler say Dobbin "was one of the bravest officers in the army." Separated easily from Amelia; she yearned "every hour of the day."

**Miniature Portrait**: Commissioned miniature of himself from own money; old Osborne doubled the sovereigns paid. Amelia hung it beside George's over her bed. Now visits mother in Gillespie Street once or twice weekly, "bullied the servants and his relations there, just as he did in Russell Square."

## Amelia's Suffering and New Life (Chapter 24–25)

**Mrs. Sedley's Death**: Few months after Georgy went to grandfather, Mrs. Sedley died. Georgy showed little grief, angered he could not attend play. Amelia closed her eyes.

**John Sedley's Destitution and Amelia's Bondage**: Old man "stunned by the blow"; only Amelia stood by him. Forced to accept Osborne's pecuniary obligations—"one of the many causes for personal pride with which old Osborne chose to recreate himself." Amelia's life "came down to this--to a mean prison and a long, ignoble bondage." Russell Square was "boundary of her prison"; she slept nightly in "cell at Brompton."

**Amelia's Devotion**: Determined "with all her might and strength to try and make her old father happy. She slaved, toiled, patched, and mended, sang and played backgammon, read out the newspaper, cooked dishes for old Sedley, walked him out sedulously into Kensington Gardens or the Brompton Lanes."

**Piano Disillusionment (Chapter 25)**: Amelia cherished old piano as "the only one which she had received from her lover"—"her dearest relic and prize." Upon discovery Dobbin bought it years ago, "It was not George's relic. It was valueless now."

**Dobbin's Declaration (Chapter 25)**: "Amelia, Amelia...I did buy it for you. I loved you then as I do now...I think there is no hour in the day has passed for twelve years that I haven't thought of you." Acknowledged her hurt at piano revelation; asked pardon "for being a fool for a moment."

**Amelia's Steadfast Refusal (Chapter 25)**: "George is my husband, here and in heaven. How could I love any other but him?...You are everything to me and my boy...our dearest, truest, kindest friend and protector." Voice broke; she hid face on his shoulder. Told Polly "never, never" to speak of remarriage; could not remarry after such an angel.

**Emotional Awareness (Chapter 25)**: Not displeased by Dobbin's attachment; would give him "friendly regard, which so much excellence and fidelity merited" and speak "when he made his proposals." Shook head sadly and wept when Jos hinted at remarriage.

## Major Dobbin's Return (Chapter 24–25)

**Illness in Madras**: Obtained leave, travelled "night and day" to Madras "in a high fever." Lay "tossing in his fever...raving about Amelia." Made testament, left property "to those whom he most desired to benefit." Wore "little brown hair-chain...from Amelia's maid at Brussels...when the young widow's hair was cut off, during the fever which prostrated her after the death of George Osborne."

**Passage on Ramchunder**: Recovered. After St. Helena, displayed "gaiety and strength." Became "impatient and ill-humoured" within ten days' sail; recovered when breeze sprang up. "Good God, how his heart beat as the two friendly spires of Southampton came in sight." Entire crew cheered at landing. Jos received cheers, took off cap "majestically."

**Journey to London**: Travelled rapidly. At Slaughters' Inn, inquired about "Captain Osborne's widow"; innkeeper John noted loan from April 1815. Chose "smartest...civil costume," laughed at "tanned face and grey hair."

**Reunion with Clapps (Chapter 25)**: Called on Clapps in Brompton; greeted by Miss Mary Polly Clapp. Identified as "old friend," Georgy's godfather. **Reverend Binny's Marriage**: Learned Binny married Miss Grits (grocer's daughter, five thousand pound fortune), returned from Margate. Dobbin's "head was swimming with felicity"—"no longer a rival to fear."

**Meeting with Amelia (Chapter 25)**: Old Sedley sat on bench "prattling away...some old story about old times." Amelia first feared something happened to Georgy; sight of messenger's happy face dissipated fear. Dobbin's "lean figure and long shadow stalking across the grass" caused her to start, blush, cry. She came "running towards him, her hands before her." "She wasn't changed. She was a little pale, a little stouter in figure. Her eyes were the same, the kind trustful eyes. There were scarce three lines of silver in her soft brown hair." He took "the two little hands between his two and held them there. He was speechless for a moment. Why did he not take her in his arms and swear that he would never leave her?"

**Tea at Sedley's Home (Chapter 25)**: Despite "particular business in London that evening," consented to tea upon Mr. Sedley's invitation. "Amelia put her arm under that of her young friend with the yellow shawl...so that Mr. Sedley fell to Dobbin's share." Old man "walked very slowly and told a number of ancient histories." Dobbin's "eyes were fixed upon the figure in front of him--the dear little figure always present to his imagination and in his prayers." Evening, "his eyes followed her about as they sat in the twilight." Amelia "laughingly encouraged it and looked exceedingly roguish as she administered to him cup after cup." Dobbin had no dinner; plate lay at Slaughters' "in that very box in which the Major and George had sat many a time carousing, when she was a child just come home from Miss Pinkerton's school." Treated himself to half-price at Haymarket Theatre that evening.

**Dobbin's Temperament**: Of "too simple and generous a nature" to harbor jealousy of young Indian officers. "Glad that the young men should pay her respect, and that others should admire her. Ever since her womanhood almost, had she not been persecuted and undervalued?" Pleased to see "kindness brought out her good qualities" and "her spirits gently rose with her prosperity." Called Swankey of Body Guard "that dangerous young buck"; Swankey described pig-sticking to Amelia with "great humour and eloquence," later spoke of "a d--d king's officer that's always hanging about the house--a long, thin, queer-looking, oldish fellow."

## Jos Sedley's Return (Chapter 25)

**Ten Years in Bengal**: Passed ten years with "Constant dinners, tiffins, pale ale and claret...the prodigious labour of cutcherry, and the refreshment of brandy-pawnee" affecting him. Served with fine appointments, laid by considerable money, returned with good pension.

**Passage**: After St. Helena, became "very generous, disposing of a great quantity of ship stores." No ladies aboard; Jos was "first dignitary at table." Disappeared "rather in a panic during a two-days' gale," remained in cot reading *The Washerwoman of Finchley Common*. Dobbin impressed "duty most strongly upon his fellow-passenger" and "extorted promises" Jos would "take charge of his sister and her child."

**Reunion**: Jos announced fatigue after voyage; spent time hiring servant, instructing agent, having waistcoats made. Upon arrival, declared "they should never suffer want or discomfort any more...Amelia would look very pretty at the head of his table--until she would accept one of her own."

## Amelia's New Household and Social Life (Chapter 25–26)

**Separation from Mary Clapp**: Mary's sorrow at departure "such as I shall not attempt to depict." From childhood, "she had been with her daily and had attached herself so passionately to that dear good lady." When barouche came, "she fainted in the arms of her friend, who was indeed scarcely less affected." Amelia loved her "like a daughter." Arranged Mary would visit. **Plan (rumor)**: "Poor Mary...was placed under the medical treatment of the young fellow from the surgery, under whose care she rallied."

**Transfer and New Household**: Emmy "endowed Mary with every article of furniture that the house contained, only taking away her pictures...and her piano." New modest household: butler was Jos's valet; Emmy supplied maid "grown on Sir William Dobbin's suburban estate"; maid's "kindness and humility disarmed Mrs. Osborne...who did not in the least know how to use one." Maid useful tending old Mr. Sedley "who kept almost entirely to his own quarter."

**Social Visits and Acceptance (Chapter 25)**: "Numbers of people came to see Mrs. Osborne." Lady Dobbin and daughters waited upon her. Miss Osborne came in grand chariot with "flaming hammer-cloth emblazoned with the Leeds arms." Jos "reported to be immensely rich." Old Osborne allowed Georgy inherit uncle's property "as well as his own." Miss Osborne invited though old Osborne said "I'll never set eyes on her." Emmy "very glad to see her...brought nearer to George."

**Daily Routines (Chapter 25–26)**: Emmy had visiting-book, drove regularly in carriage calling on Lady Bludyer, Lady Huff, Mrs. Pice, etc. "Buttony boy" sprang up and down with visiting-cards. Emmy and carriage collected Jos from Club for airing; drove old Sedley round Regent's Park. "The lady's maid and the chariot, the visiting-book and the buttony page, became soon as familiar to Amelia as the humble routine of Brompton. She accommodated herself to one as to the other." Voted "rather a pleasing young person--not much in her, but pleasing."

**Young Indian Officers**: Young Indian dandies on furlough admired Mrs. Osborne, bowed to her carriage, paid morning visits. Swankey of Body Guard discovered by Dobbin "tete-a-tete with Amelia, and describing the sport of pig-sticking to her with great humour and eloquence."

**Jos at Court (Chapter 25–26)**: After Jos went to Court in full court suit, became "such a tremendous Tory and pillar of the State" he insisted Amelia attend Drawing-room. "He somehow had worked himself up to believe that he was implicated in the maintenance of the public welfare and that the Sovereign would not be happy unless Jos Sedley and his family appeared."

## John Sedley's Final Illness and Death (Chapter 26)

**Onset of Decline**: Shortly after Mrs. Sedley's death and Jos's return, old man "was about to go seek for his wife in the dark land whither she had preceded him." Jos remarked at Club: "The state of my father's health prevents me from giving any LARGE parties this season: but if you will come in quietly at half-past six...I shall be always glad to see you." Jos and acquaintances dined and drank claret "whilst the sands of life were running out in the old man's glass upstairs."

**Amelia's Nursing**: Old man "clung to his daughter during this sickness...scarcely any other hand" gave him broths and medicines. "To tend him became almost the sole business of her life." Her bed placed close to his chamber door; "she was alive at the slightest noise or disturbance from the couch of the querulous invalid." Though he "lay awake many an hour, silent and without stirring, unwilling to awaken his kind and vigilant nurse."

**Love and Devotion**: Loved daughter "with more fondness now, perhaps, than ever he had done since the days of her childhood. In the discharge of gentle offices and kind filial duties, this simple creature shone most especially." Dobbin observed: "She walks into the room as silently as a sunbeam...a cheerful sweetness lighting up her face as she moved to and fro, graceful and noiseless. When women are brooding over their children, or busied in a sick-room, who has not seen in their faces those sweet angelic beams of love and pity?"
